item.title: Poker Taught Me to Stop Confusing Good Decisions With Good Outcomes
item.description:
I spent part of my professional life playing poker for a living. A few of the lessons stuck, and I still use them in product leadership and when working with startups.

The biggest one: you can make the right decision and still lose.

You can put your money in with the best hand and watch the river complete some ridiculous draw. Same thing in business. You can correctly identify a real customer problem, build the right solution, and still watch the launch fail because of timing, competition, or pure bad luck.

item.title: Stop hunting for PMF. Start diagnosing the fit.
item.description:
As a founder, how often have you said to yourself:

“We need to find product-market fit.”

Fair enough.

But often, that isn’t really the problem.

The harder problem is figuring out what exactly needs to fit what.

A product can fail to find traction for very different reasons:

  • The product is technically possible, but nobody really needs it.
  • People need it, but not enough to pay for it.
  • People will pay, but the economics don’t work.
  • There is demand, but the founder has no particular advantage in serving it.

These are very different problems.

item.title: The Product Market Fit Primer
item.description:
Product Market Fit becomes easier to reason about when broad conviction is translated into specific questions: who the audience is, what problem matters, what customers do today, where the economic value comes from, why they would pay, and which assumptions could invalidate the idea.

Is there a specific customer who needs this badly enough to pay for it?

This is a working document. The frameworks establish a structure; the exercises challenge your assumptions; the worksheets make you apply the thinking to your own product. Customer discovery and validation tools help you distinguish belief from evidence. The final output is a Product Market Fit hypothesis you can actually test.

item.title: Old Code, Old Thinking
item.description:
I went back into some old code recently (The Feature That Killed the Project Wasn’t a Bad Feature), and found something interesting.

The code itself hasn’t aged particularly well. That’s probably inevitable. Dependencies are old, some things are half-built, and there are parts I’d approach very differently today.

But the thinking behind it has aged surprisingly well.

I’m still quite proud of the hand comparison logic I wrote. I’ve cited it on public forums a few times when I’ve come across someone building a poker app and struggling with hand evaluation.

item.title: A Recommendation Without a CTA
item.description:
My work neighbour ordered a chicken meal the other day.

When the food arrived, I noticed a small section printed on the package.

“Try Next”

Under it were pictures and names of two other chicken dishes.

That’s it.

No QR code. No discount. No “Order now”. No elaborate loyalty programme.

Just two little suggestions for the next time.

And I thought: this is a brilliant piece of product thinking.

item.title: Zero Trust Gives a Better Experience Than Low Trust
item.description:
This morning I had to leave home while our new cleaning staff was still working.

I could have stayed around and kept an eye on things. After all, I don’t know them well yet.

Instead, I locked one of the rooms, told them about it, and left.

They had access to everything they needed to do their job. I had protected the one space they didn’t need access to. When they finished, they would close the main door behind them.

item.title: The Feature That Killed the Project Wasn't a Bad Feature
item.description:
Around 2020, a friend and I started building an online multiplayer poker application.

The idea was straightforward enough. Create a private table, invite your friends, sit down together and play Texas Hold’em in the browser. I had spent years playing poker professionally, so the game logic was familiar territory. We built the table, cards, player seating, multiplayer state and a fair amount of the poker engine. We had hand comparison working. My friend was working through pots and side pots, including the genuinely unpleasant edge cases created by multiple all-ins.

item.title: A Quick Test for A Startup Idea: Focus
item.description:
Find:

  1. One thing you can do exceptionally well.
  2. One slice of users who care enough about it.
  3. A large enough market at that intersection.
  4. A quick MVP you can put in front of them and start learning from.

Then move.

If you keep dithering on any of these dimensions, what you’re probably dealing with isn’t execution complexity. It’s an unresolved business model.

Go back and rethink it.

–

Working through a similar product challenge?

item.title: Help, I'm Turning Into a Services Company!
item.description:
A few years apart, I found myself having the same argument in two very different companies.

In the first, a client came to us with an existing software package. They needed two junior developers to maintain it.

The commercial arrangement was simple: they paid us the salaries of those two people, plus what can generously be described as loose change.

I wasn’t enthusiastic.

My concern wasn’t that the work was beneath us. Someone had a system that needed maintaining. They were willing to pay for it. Fair enough.

item.title: The Startup Red Flag I Look For: When Technology Becomes the Product
item.description:
One of the first things I look for when evaluating a startup is deceptively simple:

What is the technology actually doing for the customer?

Not what it could do.

Not how technically impressive it is.

Not whether the founders have built something that would make an engineer excited.

What does it actually change for the person paying for it?

This matters because I see a recurring pattern in startups, particularly AI startups.

item.title: About Amit
item.description:
Hi, I’m Amit Sharma.

I build digital products, help founders build better ones, and spend a lot of time thinking about how technology changes the way we solve problems.

Over the last 18 years, I’ve worked across fintech, insurance, wealth management, education, consumer products, and SaaS. My career has taken me from large organizations like ICICI Securities to high-growth startups like Coverfox, and today to working independently as a fractional product leader, startup advisor, mentor, and educator.

item.title: Speaking
item.description:
Talks for people building products in the real world

01 · Why Founders Overbuild Before They Overlearn

Capable founders often respond to uncertainty by building more. This session examines how to tell development activity from real learning about what customers need and will pay for.

Audience takeaways:

  • Identify the riskiest customer and business assumptions behind a product idea.
  • Separate evidence of customer learning from evidence that a team has shipped.
  • Choose a useful next validation step before committing to more build work.

02 · Product Decisions When Everything Seems Important

For early-stage founders, product leaders and operators balancing competing demands with limited time and resources. Explore prioritisation, stakeholder pressure and execution bottlenecks, and the discipline required to make consequential choices.
